items.questionAndWhy: What makes people willing to support unfamiliar carbon-removal projects: their technical performance, or how decisions and benefits are shared? The answer matters before large projects are sited and contested.
items.whatTheyDid: Fritz and colleagues ran multifactorial vignette experiments in nationally representative surveys across Brazil, Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, Italy, Norway, and the UK (10,852 respondents). People evaluated projects varying the implementing actor, consultation, profit distribution, and removal capacity.
items.whatTheyFound: Consulting local people or experts increased support by about 1.0–1.7 points on a ten-point scale relative to no consultation. Community benefit sharing and public-service arrangements also raised support. Higher removal capacity helped, but generally did not compensate for unfair procedures or distribution. These are stated responses to hypothetical projects, not observed acceptance of built facilities.
items.whatItMeans: Legitimacy is part of implementation, not a communications add-on. A model of technology adoption should represent decision process, trust, and who receives benefits separately from technical performance; field settings may produce stronger conflict than these unfamiliar vignettes.

items.questionAndWhy: When a sustainable choice costs money, does moral disengagement appear only afterward as an excuse, or is it already associated with the choice? This distinguishes a prior orientation from post-choice rationalization.
items.whatTheyDid: Yakut and Laurent conducted four studies with 817 participants, using financial-environmental choice scenarios, measures of positive beliefs about greed and moral disengagement, and assessments of pride and guilt. One study measured disengagement before and after decisions across a 15-day interval.
items.whatTheyFound: Positive beliefs about greed and moral disengagement were associated with more self-interested, environmentally harmful choices. Disengagement was relatively stable before and after a choice, and shaped emotional reactions. Several studies were correlational, so the paper does not establish that changing disengagement would cause a different real-world choice.
items.whatItMeans: The same stated environmental concern can coexist with different norms about self-interest and different emotional responses. Assess these factors alongside actual costs; avoid assuming a post-choice justification is the only mechanism or that a vignette predicts sustained behavior.

items.questionAndWhy: Which part of an engagement-based recommendation score might help low-credibility content spread, and would merely adjusting weights fix it?
items.whatTheyDid: Li and Gao inspected publicly released X recommendation code, reimplemented a ranking component on a 2024 election-post corpus, and simulated exposure under alternative scoring rules. They labeled linked domains by source credibility and ran 46 robustness checks.
items.whatTheyFound: In their model, predicted likes and reposts could substitute for replies and quotes in a weighted engagement score, favoring content that elicited quick reactions. Weight tuning had little or adverse effect in simulations; a threshold requiring predicted reflective engagement reduced the low-credibility exposure gap without reducing modeled mainstream exposure or engagement. This is an unreviewed preprint and a calibrated reimplementation, not a live platform intervention.
items.whatItMeans: A ranking system can shape exposure through the way it combines behavior signals, even if no single signal is explicitly labeled as misinformation. Platform-level causal claims require live validation and careful treatment of source-credibility labels.

items.questionAndWhy: Can a model that checks written claims reliably verify speech, and does adding retrieved text solve the problem?
items.whatTheyDid: Mazumder and colleagues built VeriSpeak, a benchmark of 3,879 spoken claims about temporal, geographic, and relational facts, balanced between true and false labels. They tested large audio-language models with retrieval and explicit claim-evidence reasoning.
items.whatTheyFound: The authors report a persistent text-to-speech performance gap. Retrieval alone gave limited gains because models sometimes conflated evidence with the spoken claim; retrieval plus explicit reasoning performed better, with one reasoning-tuned model reaching 86.1% accuracy. The benchmark uses controlled factual claims, so these results do not establish reliability on noisy political speeches or real-time podcasts.
items.whatItMeans: Audio fact checking needs more than transcription plus retrieval. Test claim extraction, evidence comparison, and speech-specific errors separately before using a system to label live influence content.

items.questionAndWhy: Can AI judges consistently score conversational success, especially across different judges and spoken human-AI interactions?
items.whatTheyDid: Züfle and colleagues compared pointwise and pairwise LLM judgments against human ratings on CANDOR conversations. They proposed a small anchor set for calibration and released Voice Arena Goal, 200 task-oriented human-AI and human-agent conversations with pairwise annotations.
items.whatTheyFound: Pointwise scores correlated moderately with human ratings, while pairwise comparisons suffered from long transcripts and position bias. The new dataset showed a gap between current judges and human discrimination. Calibration placed judges on a shared scale and transferred to the human-AI dataset in their tests; it did not make the judges equivalent to human evaluators.
items.whatItMeans: Evaluation scores should carry a calibration protocol and a human reference. In PSYWERX-style human-AI assessments, compare stable anchor cases and inspect order effects before treating score differences as substantive.

items.questionAndWhy: How should an analyst combine inexpensive but imperfect AI labels with human verification when the end result is a formal statistical decision?
items.whatTheyDid: Ham and colleagues modeled a fixed pool of items with hidden binary labels. Their SCALE policy can query AI, request a human judgment, escalate an AI-scored item, or stop as evidence accumulates. They derive a cost lower bound, analyze error control, and simulate cost under different AI-human conditions.
items.whatTheyFound: The authors prove finite-sample validity under their model and show near-optimal asymptotic cost as target errors tighten. Numerical studies found the largest savings when cheap AI reports and selective human checks both contributed. These are formal and simulated results, not evidence of savings or accuracy in a deployed PSYWERX review queue.
items.whatItMeans: Human review is most useful where the AI report changes the value of verification. A pilot with paired human and AI labels would be needed to estimate the error model and test whether the theoretical saving transfers to an actual research workflow.

items.questionAndWhy: How can 32 allies connect sensors, decisions, and capabilities across domains quickly enough to act together during disruption?
items.whatTheyDid: NATO Allied Command Transformation published an account of its multi-domain operations approach, describing orchestration across land, air, sea, space, and cyber activities alongside relevant non-military activity. It emphasizes shared data, national control of assets, standards, training, and resilient connections.
items.whatTheyFound: The publication lays out an operational approach and implementation logic: interoperability and resilience must be built and exercised before crisis, while nations retain authority over what they share. It reports no controlled comparison or measured advantage from a new deployment. Its discussion of the cognitive dimension is conceptual rather than an observed influence effect.
items.whatItMeans: For information advantage, speed is an end-to-end property of sensing, sharing, deciding, and acting, subject to governance and trust. Evaluation should test degraded communications, data-sharing permissions, and cross-national handoffs rather than count connected tools alone.

items.questionAndWhy: How can researchers track media framing over decades without treating automated labels as equally reliable across categories?
items.whatTheyDid: Lemor and colleagues assembled 283,964 climate-related articles from 22 Canadian news outlets spanning 1978–2026, split into roughly 9.9 million two-sentence units. They trained 128 English and French classifiers from more than 4,000 expert-coded sentences to assign 65 hierarchical labels and published article aggregations and embeddings.
items.whatTheyFound: On a 1,000-sentence independently double-coded reference set, the pooled macro F1 was 0.866, while mean per-category macro F1 was 0.773; categories were assigned A/B/C reliability tiers. These metrics describe annotation performance, not proof of media effects on public opinion. Coverage is Canadian and source selection matters.
items.whatItMeans: The corpus is a useful design pattern for PSYWERX discourse maps: publish a taxonomy, human coding reference, category-specific uncertainty, and reusable data together. Trend analyses should account for changing outlet coverage and weaker classes.

items.questionAndWhy: When a multi-stage AI video system gives a wrong answer, is the dominant cause locating the wrong clip, observing it badly, or reasoning badly afterward?
items.whatTheyDid: Gong and colleagues compared benchmark scores with stage interventions that replaced temporal grounding, visual observations, or reasoning inputs while keeping downstream tasks fixed. Their experiments covered 60,008 runs across three video-agent architectures.
items.whatTheyFound: In those tested systems, grounding had roughly four times the downstream causal impact of corrupted visual observations. Finding the right region mattered more than tight temporal overlap, and wrong evidence caused more harm than missing evidence. Stage benchmark scores did not consistently predict these cascading effects. The preprint's controlled interventions do not show the same proportions for every video system or field workflow.
items.whatItMeans: For video-based incident analysis, log which segment a model used and audit retrieval failures separately from final answer quality. A high aggregate score can hide a failure in the evidence path.

items.questionAndWhy: Do prominent nutrition and health claims on newly launched products reliably indicate better overall nutritional quality?
items.whatTheyDid: Zhou and colleagues analyzed newly launched US food and beverage products in the Mintel Global New Products Database. They compared four classes of on-package claims with scores under the UK nutrient profiling model and examined claim types and product categories.
items.whatTheyFound: Products with claims sometimes had more favorable profiles in aggregate, but the pattern varied. Foods with trans-fat claims and beverages with sodium claims often scored worse than peers without them; many claim-bearing products still counted as less healthy overall. The study measured products, not how consumers interpreted labels or changed purchases.
items.whatItMeans: A salient attribute can be an imperfect proxy for the full outcome. Communication and evaluation should distinguish the specific true claim from the broader inference audiences may draw; behavioral effects need separate testing.
